analysis.one_liner: Extends the military's 36% interest rate cap on consumer loans to all Americans.
analysis.headline: The bill that would cap consumer loan interest at 36% — the same protection servicemembers already get — was heard three times in committee but never came to a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Servicemembers and their families are already protected by a federal law that caps most consumer loan interest at 36% and restricts fees and add-on products. This bill would have extended those same protections to every borrower: payday loans, installment loans, and credit cards would all have been subject to the cap. The bill never got a vote — it was referred to the Senate Banking Committee, discussed in three hearings, and expired when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary borrowers who use high-cost credit — people taking out payday loans that can carry triple-digit annual rates, installment loans, and credit cards with high rates and expensive add-on fees. Veterans, who the bill is named for, are a major group affected since the cap stops applying once they leave the service.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Payday, installment, and high-rate card borrowers

how_it_helps.text: Caps the interest rate on consumer credit at 36% annual percentage rate for all borrowers, using the same protections servicemembers receive under the Military Lending Act [S2] [S3].

Applies the Military Lending Act's rules against fees and credit add-on products — such as credit insurance and debt suspension agreements — to all consumer credit, not just loans to military families [S3].
Requires the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau to write rules carrying out the cap, and bars the Bureau from granting exemptions from the rate limit [S3].
Preserves state laws that go further, and lets state attorneys general and state regulators enforce the federal cap in court [S3].
Gives borrowers the same remedies as under the Military Lending Act, including penalties against creditors who violate the cap [S3].

analysis.who_pays: High-cost lenders — payday and installment lenders, and credit card issuers whose effective rates or fees exceed the cap — lose the revenue they earn on interest and fees above 36%. Some subprime borrowers may find fewer lenders willing to extend them credit at all.

drawbacks.text: The cap exempts home mortgages, car-purchase loans secured by the car, and federal credit union loans — so the largest kinds of consumer debt are left largely untouched, and lenders can steer borrowers into car financing to avoid the cap [S3].

Lenders who depend on high rates to cover the risk of lending to borrowers with poor credit may stop lending to them entirely, leaving some borrowers with no access to small-dollar credit instead of expensive access — the main objection raised in hearings about rate caps.
With most consumers' existing credit-card rates below 36%, the cap's biggest immediate effect would fall on a smaller set of very high-rate products, limiting its reach compared with a broader cap.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade-off is real: a 36% cap would sharply cut the cost of payday and other small-dollar loans for millions of borrowers, but it would also shrink the supply of credit to the riskiest borrowers, some of whom would lose access to loans altogether rather than get cheaper ones. The bill also leaves mortgages, car loans, and credit unions exempt, narrowing its scope. On balance the benefit to ordinary borrowers is large and the cost is concentrated on a small set of lenders and the highest-risk borrowers.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate Banking Committee — which held hearings on it but never voted on a final version — and expired when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Senator Jack Reed introduced the Veterans and Consumers Fair Credit Act on July 28, 2021 with 14 Democratic cosponsors [S1] [S3] [S4].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs [S5].
The Banking Committee held hearings on the bill in July 2021, January 2022, and September 2022, but the full committee never voted to send it to the Senate floor [S5].
All 14 cosponsors were Democrats; no Senate Republicans signed on, and the bill was never brought to a vote in either chamber [S4].
The bill expired with the 117th Congress in January 2023 without a vote; similar versions would have to be reintroduced in a new Congress [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High-cost lenders — payday, installment, and high-fee credit card issuers — are better off, since the 36% cap never became law and their current rates and fees remain legal. Borrowers who would have qualified for cheaper loans are worse off.

sides.party_line_note: All 14 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican supported the bill, so it never had the bipartisan backing needed to move in the Senate.

industries.note: The 36% cap would make their core product — loans carrying triple-digit annual rates — illegal for the general market. Their revenue comes directly from interest above the cap, so their gain is borrowers' loss.

Most cards would already comply with a 36% rate cap, but the bill applies the military rules on fees and blocks add-on products like credit insurance and debt suspension fees, cutting into card revenue on high-rate and fee-heavy accounts.
Credit union loans are explicitly exempt from the cap, keeping their lower-rate products available while their main competitors in small-dollar lending face the 36% limit.

industries.industry: Mortgage lenders and auto finance companies
industries.note: Their products are exempted from the cap, so none of its costs touch them — but they also gain nothing from the protections.
